newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Arabs watch Jews take over East Jerusalem house.
newsitem.headline: Arabs watch Jews take over East Jerusalem house.

text.p: Palestinians glumly watched Jewish settlers take over a sprawling building complex in an Arab East Jerusalem neighbourhood on Thursday.
A Jewish woman sunned herself behind a gate manned by a phalanx of burly Israeli private security guards armed with automatic pistols and crackling walkie-talkies.

Settler men wearing the skullcaps and fringed undershirts of religious Jews did minor repairs to the building in the neighbourhood of 30,000 Palestinians in the shadow of East Jerusalem's walled Old City.
"This isn't the first time they have exploited a tense situation to take over homes in Silwan," resident Majed Karain told Reuters.

He recalled settlers last took over a Silwan home on September 24, a day before unprecedented clashes erupted in the West Bank and Gaza over Israel's punching a second opening into a tourist tunnel near Moslem holy sites in Jerusalem's Old City.
Sixty-one Palestinians and 15 Israeli soldiers were killed in the several days of fighting.
This time, the five families moved in as Israeli bulldozers for a third day cleared land for the new Jewish settlement of Har Homa at Jerusalem's southern outskirts.
The latest settlement building stopped Israeli-Palestinian peace moves in their tracks and spawned clashes.
In 1991 a first group of settlers took over houses in Silwan where they say the biblical King David built the first capital of the Jewish people.
Settler spokesman Yigal Canaan told Reuters at Silwan that 18 Jewish families now lived in the hilly neighbourhood.
Canaan said all the houses taken over by the settlers were legally acquired. Israeli peace activists and Palestinians have long disputed the claim.
"This whole hill is part of ancient Jerusalem and our organisation's goal is for the whole hill to become Jewish," he said. The hill runs through the middle of Silwan.
Palestinians milled in the street and stood on rooftops overlooking the new settler complex. One came out of his home and offered journalists glasses of sweet tea on a tray.
Abed Qaraeen, 30, a father of six, said he was worried.
"I think they're trying to add fuel to the fire," he said.
